paragraphs: Alyosha entered his elder’s cell with an anxious, aching heart, and he stopped in the doorway, almost astonished. He had been afraid of finding a sick man at his last gasp, perhaps unconscious. Instead the elder was sitting up in his chair. He was weak and worn out, yet his face was bright and cheerful. Visitors were gathered around him, and they were talking together quietly and happily. In fact he had left his bed only a quarter of an hour before Alyosha came. The visitors had assembled in his cell earlier and sat waiting for him to wake. Father Païssy had assured them with great confidence that “the teacher would get up and, as he had promised that morning, talk once more with those dear to his heart.” Father Païssy trusted this promise completely, as he trusted every word the dying elder spoke. Suppose he had found him unconscious, or even seen him breathe his last, and still held his promise that he would rise and say good-bye. Perhaps even then he would not have believed in death. He would have gone on expecting the dead man to revive and keep his word. That morning, as he lay down to sleep, Father Zossima had told him flatly: “I shall not die without the joy of one more conversation with you, beloved of my heart. I shall look once more on your dear face and pour out my heart to you again.” The monks who had gathered for this probably last talk with Father Zossima had been his devoted friends for many years. There were four of them. The first two were Father Iosif and Father Païssy. The third was Father Mihaïl, warden of the hermitage, a man not very old and far from learned. He came of humble people, and he had a strong will and a steadfast faith. He looked austere, but he was deeply tender, though he clearly kept this hidden, as if almost ashamed of it. The fourth, Father Anfim, was a very old, humble little monk from the poorest peasant class. He was nearly illiterate and very quiet, and he hardly spoke to anyone. He was the humblest of the humble, and he looked as if something vast and terrible, beyond his understanding, had frightened him. Father Zossima was deeply fond of this timid man and always treated him with marked respect. Yet perhaps he had said less to him than to anyone he had ever known, although he had spent years wandering with him over holy Russia. That was long ago, forty years back, when Father Zossima was just beginning his monastic life in a poor little monastery at Kostroma. Soon afterward he had gone with Father Anfim on a journey to collect alms for that poor monastery.

They were all in the bedroom, which, as we said before, was very small. There was hardly room for the four of them to sit round Father Zossima on chairs brought in from the sitting room (Porfiry the novice stood). Darkness was already coming on. The room was lit by lamps and by the candles in front of the ikons.
Seeing Alyosha standing embarrassed in the doorway, Father Zossima smiled at him joyfully and held out his hand.
“Welcome, my quiet one. Welcome, my dear, you are here too. I knew you would come.”
Alyosha went to him and bowed to the ground before him, and he wept. Something rose up from deep in his heart. His soul was shaking, and he wanted to sob aloud.

“Come now, do not weep over me yet,” said Father Zossima with a smile, laying his right hand on Alyosha’s head. “You see, I am sitting up and talking. Maybe I shall live another twenty years, as that good dear woman from Vishegorye wished me yesterday, with her little Lizaveta in her arms. God bless the mother and the little girl Lizaveta.” He crossed himself. “Porfiry, did you take her offering where I told you?”

He meant the sixty copecks that the cheerful woman had brought him the day before, to be passed on “to someone poorer than me.” Gifts like this are always made from money earned by one’s own labor, and they are offered as a penance freely chosen. The previous evening the elder had sent Porfiry to a widow whose house had recently burned down, and who had been going about begging with her children since the fire. Porfiry quickly replied that he had handed over the money as instructed, “from an unknown benefactress.”

“Get up, my dear boy,” the elder went on, speaking to Alyosha. “I want to look at you. Have you been home? Did you see your brother?” Alyosha thought it strange that he asked so confidently and so exactly about just one of his brothers. But which one? Perhaps he had sent Alyosha out yesterday and again today for that brother’s sake.
“I have seen one of my brothers,” answered Alyosha.
“I mean the elder one, the one I bowed down to.”
“I only saw him yesterday. I could not find him today,” said Alyosha.

“Hurry and find him. Go again tomorrow, and hurry. Drop everything and hurry. You may still be in time to prevent something terrible. Yesterday I bowed down before the great suffering that awaits him.”

He fell silent all at once and seemed lost in thought. His words were strange. Father Iosif, who had seen the scene the day before, exchanged a look with Father Païssy. Alyosha could not keep himself from asking:
“Father and teacher,” he began, deeply moved, “your words are too dark to me.... What is this suffering that awaits him?”

“Do not ask. Yesterday I seemed to see something terrible ... as if his whole future were written in his eyes. There came a look into his eyes—and I was struck with horror at once, at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I have seen that look on a man’s face ... showing, as it were, the fate in store for him, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought the sight of a brother’s face would help him. But everything, and all our fates, come from the Lord. ‘Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. As for you, Alexey, many times I have blessed you silently because of your face. Know that,” added the elder, with a gentle smile. “This is what I think of you. You will leave these walls, but you will live in the world like a monk. You will have many enemies, yet even your enemies will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but in them you will find your happiness, and you will bless life and make others bless it, which is what matters most. Well, that is your character. Fathers and teachers,” he said to his friends with a tender smile, “until today I have never told even him why this young man’s face is so dear to me. Now I will tell you. His face has been for me a remembrance and a prophecy together. When I was a child, at the dawn of my life, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at the age of seventeen. As my life went on, I gradually came to believe that this brother was meant as a guide and a sign from above for me. Had he not entered my life, I should never have become a monk and set foot on this precious path, or so I think. He appeared to me first in my childhood, and now, at the end of my pilgrimage, it seems he has come to me a second time. It is marvelous, fathers and teachers. Alexey bears some resemblance to him in face, though not a great one. But in spirit he seems to me so like him that many times I have taken him for that young man, my brother, come back to me mysteriously at the end of my journey to remind and inspire me. I was truly amazed at so strange a fancy in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” He turned to the novice who attended him. “Many times I have seen a look of hurt in your face, because I love Alexey more than you. Now you know the reason. But I love you too, know that, and many times I was grieved by your hurt. Dear friends, I want to tell you about that youth, my brother, for no one who has been in my life was more precious, more full of meaning, or more touching. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I look at my whole life as though I were living it over again.”

Here I must point out that this last conversation of Father Zossima with the friends who visited him on the last day of his life has been partly preserved in writing. Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov put it down from memory, some time after his elder’s death. Whether it was only the talk of that evening, or whether he also wove in notes from earlier conversations with his teacher, I cannot say. In his account Father Zossima speaks on without a break, as if he were telling his life to his friends as a story. Yet other accounts leave no doubt that the talk that evening was shared by all. The guests did not interrupt Father Zossima often, but they did talk, and perhaps they even told some stories of their own. Besides, Father Zossima could not have gone on without pause. He sometimes gasped for breath and lost his voice, and he even lay down on his bed to rest, though he did not sleep, and his visitors stayed in their seats. Once or twice Father Païssy broke in to read from the Gospel. It is also worth noting that not one of them thought he would die that night. In the evening, after his deep sleep during the day, he seemed to have suddenly found fresh strength, and it carried him through this long conversation. It was like a last effort of love, and it gave him marvelous energy. It lasted only a short time, however, for his life was cut short at once.... But of that later. For now I will add only that I have chosen to keep to the account written by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. It will be shorter and less wearying, though, as I must say again, Alyosha took much from earlier conversations and added it here.
Notes on the Life of the late Priest and Monk, the Elder Zossima, taken down from his own words by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.
BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES
_(a)_ _Father Zossima’s Brother_

Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a remote northern province, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but he had no great standing or rank. He died when I was two years old, and I have no memory of him at all. He left my mother a small house built of wood and a modest fortune, but enough to keep her and her children comfortably. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and I. He was eight years older than I was. He had a hasty, irritable temper, but he was kind-hearted and never sneering. He was remarkably silent, especially at home, with me, with his mother and with the servants. He did well at school but could not get along with his schoolmates, though he never fought with them, or so my mother has told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile. This man had been sent from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and he lived there alone. He was a fine scholar who had distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something drew him to Markel, and he often asked him to visit. That winter the young man spent whole evenings with him, until the exile was called to Petersburg to take up his post again, at his own request, since he had powerful friends.

It was the start of Lent, and Markel would not fast. He was rude and laughed at it. “It is all silly nonsense, and there is no God,” he said, to the horror of my mother, the servants, and me as well. Though I was only nine, I was appalled at hearing such words. We had four servants, all serfs. I remember my mother selling one of them, the cook Afimya, a lame elderly woman, for sixty paper roubles, and hiring a free servant in her place.

In the sixth week of Lent my brother fell ill. He had never been strong and was prone to consumption. He was tall but thin and frail-looking, with a very pleasing face. I suppose he had caught cold. In any case, the doctor who came soon whispered to my mother that it was galloping consumption and that he would not live out the spring. My mother began to weep. She was careful not to alarm my brother, but she begged him to go to church, to confess and to receive the sacrament, since he could still get about. This angered him, and he said something profane about the church. Still, he grew thoughtful. He guessed at once that he was gravely ill, and that this was why his mother was pleading with him to confess and take the sacrament. In fact he had known for a long time that he was far from well. A year earlier he had remarked coolly at dinner, to our mother and me, “I will not be long among you. I may not live another year.” Now those words seemed like a prophecy.

Three days went by, and Holy Week arrived. On Tuesday morning my brother began going to church. “I am doing this only for you, mother, to please and comfort you,” he said. My mother wept for joy and for grief. “His end must be near,” she thought, “if he has changed so much.” But he could not go to church for long. He took to his bed, and so he had to confess and receive the sacrament at home.

Easter came late that year, and the days were bright and fine and full of fragrance. I remember that he coughed all night and slept badly, but in the morning he dressed and tried to sit in an armchair. That is how I remember him, sitting there sweet and gentle, smiling, his face bright and joyful in spite of his illness. A marvelous change had come over him, and his spirit seemed transformed. The old nurse would come in and say, “Let me light the lamp before the holy image, my dear.” Earlier he would not have let her, and would have blown it out.
“Light it, light it, dear. I was a wretch to stop you before. You are praying when you light the lamp, and I am praying when I rejoice to see you. So we are praying to the same God.”

We thought those words strange, and mother would go to her room and weep. But when she went in to him she dried her eyes and looked cheerful. “Mother, do not weep, my darling,” he would say. “I have a long life ahead of me, a long time to rejoice with you, and life is glad and joyful.”
“Oh, my dear boy, how can you speak of joy when you lie feverish all night, coughing as if you would tear yourself apart?”
“Do not cry, mother,” he would answer. “Life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we refuse to see it. If we wanted to, heaven would be on earth by tomorrow.”

Everyone marveled at what he said, so strange and sure was his way of speaking. We were all moved, and we wept. Friends came to see us. “Dear ones,” he would say to them, “what have I done to deserve your love? How can you love someone like me? And how was it that I never knew, and never valued it before?”

Whenever the servants came in, he would keep saying, “Dear, kind people, why do you do so much for me? Do I deserve to be waited on? If it were God’s will that I should live, I would wait on you, for we should all wait on one another.”
Mother shook her head as she listened. “My darling, it is your illness that makes you talk like this.”

“Mother, darling,” he would say, “there have to be servants and masters. But if so, I will be the servant of my servants, just as they are to me. And there is something else, mother. Each one of us has sinned against all men, and I more than any.”

Mother actually smiled at this, smiled through her tears. “How could you have sinned against all men, and more than all? Robbers and murderers have done that. But what sin have you committed yet, that you hold yourself more guilty than everyone?”

“Mother, little heart of mine,” he said (he had begun to use such strange, tender words then), “little heart of mine, my joy, believe me, each of us is truly responsible to all men, for all men and for everything. I cannot explain it to you, but I feel that it is so, even painfully. And how could we go on living as we did, getting angry and not knowing?”
So he rose each day, more sweet and joyful and loving than the day before. Then the doctor would come, an old German named Eisenschmidt:
“Well, doctor, do I have another day in this world?” he would ask, joking.
“You will have many days yet,” the doctor would answer, “and months and years too.”

“Months and years!” he would cry. “Why reckon in days? One day is enough for a man to know all happiness. My dear ones, why do we quarrel, and try to outdo each other, and nurse grudges? Let us go straight out to the garden and walk and play there, and love and value and kiss one another, and glorify life.”
“Your son cannot last long,” the doctor told my mother, as she went with him to the door. “The illness is reaching his brain.”

The windows of his room opened onto the garden. It was a shady garden with old trees, which were just coming into bud. The first birds of spring were fluttering in the branches and chirping and singing at his windows. As he watched them and admired them, he suddenly began to beg their forgiveness as well: “Birds of heaven, happy birds, forgive me, for I have sinned against you too.” None of us could understand that then, but he wept tears of joy. “Yes,” he said, “God’s glory was all around me, in birds, trees, meadows and sky. Only I lived in shame, dishonoring it all, and I never noticed the beauty and the glory.”
